title: About half the CO₂ we emit stays in the air, and it piled up to a record in 2025
body: On 27 October 2026 the World Meteorological Organization reported in its [Greenhouse Gas Bulletin](https://wmo.int/node/39151) that carbon dioxide in the air averaged a record 426.8 parts per million (ppm) in 2025, 2.8 ppm more than a year before and 53% above the level of 1750. Picture the air as a bathtub: burning coal, oil and gas pours CO₂ in, plants on land and the ocean drain out about half of each year's emissions, and the rest stays, affecting the climate for decades and even centuries, so it piles up. The yearly rise has tripled since the 1960s, from 0.8 ppm a year to 2.4 ppm a year in 2011–2020, and from 2023 to 2024 it jumped by 3.5 ppm, the most since measurements began in 1957, when a strong El Niño brought drought and wildfires that weakened the land's drain. The level only stops rising when what goes in falls to what the drains take out.

slides.question: In 2025, how many of every million molecules of dry air were carbon dioxide (CO₂)?
slides.explanation: About 427: the global average was 426.8 parts per million, the World Meteorological Organization reported on 27 October 2026, 53% more than in 1750.

slides.alt: Animation on a pale tiled wall: a card reads 426.8 ppm, four rust dots in a grid of 10,000, 1750 against 2025. A bathtub fills from a tap of CO₂ while green land and blue ocean drains take half. Bars of yearly rises: 0.8, 2.4, 3.5 in an El Niño, 2.8. Then the tap turns down to half.
slides.music: “Heart of Nowhere” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Turn the tap down. At what share of 2025’s emissions does the CO₂ level in the air stop rising?
slides.takeaway: At 50%: the level holds steady only when emissions fall to what land and ocean take up. Cut them by a fifth and it still rises, just more slowly.

slides.heading: How much CO₂ in the air rose in one year, in parts per million
slides.note: World Meteorological Organization, Greenhouse Gas Bulletins of 2025 and 2026.

left.label: Emissions
left.text: What people put into the air in a year, mostly by burning coal, oil and gas. Land and ocean take up about half of it.

right.label: Concentration
right.text: How much has built up in the air: 426.8 parts per million of CO₂ in 2025. The World Meteorological Organization's bulletin tracks this one.

slides.heading: Why some years jump
slides.text: The drains are not fixed. In the strong El Niño of 2023 and 2024, drought, drier plants and more wildfires weakened the land's uptake, so more CO₂ stayed in the air. Warmer seawater also dissolves less CO₂. So the rise was 3.5 ppm one year and 2.8 ppm the next, while the burning of fossil fuels went on.

slides.question: CO₂ rose 3.5 ppm from 2023 to 2024 but 2.8 ppm from 2024 to 2025. What made the second rise smaller?
options: Plants on land took up more again
slides.explanation: Oksana Tarasova of the World Meteorological Organization said the land's carbon sinks recovered and fires released less carbon in 2025, after the strong El Niño of 2023/2024.
